source.title: Relative Geometry of Neural Forecasters: Linking Accuracy and Alignment in Learned Latent Geometry
source.authors: Deniz Küçükahmetler; Maximilian Jean Hemmann; Julian Mosig von Aehrenfeld; Maximilian Amthor; Christian Deubel; Nico Scherf; Diaaeldin Taha

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports family-specific alignment, cases of accurate forecasting with weaker alignment, and results that vary by architecture and system. These results qualify broad convergence claims; it does not sweep model scale.
record.gate_note: The paper reports numerical alignment scores, family-level alignment patterns, stitching outcomes, and sensitivity to the number of anchors and similarity metric. It does not test convergence as models grow, cross-modal alignment, or recurring interpretable features. Hyperparameter-search scores are not included as findings here.
record.test_reason: Different architectures trained on the same dynamical-systems data are compared by cross-forecaster alignment of relative embeddings and by encoder–decoder stitching. This is a new setting (small forecasters on simulated systems) with results on cross-model alignment (V7), interchangeability (V4) and measure dependence (V6). There is no scale sweep, no cross-modal test and no feature-level comparison. The paper does not argue against the hypothesis, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that anchor-based relative embeddings reveal reproducible, family-specific representational geometries in neural forecasters. Alignment generally tracks forecasting accuracy, but high accuracy can coexist with low alignment (transformers, ESNs). Alignment is presented as a complement to task loss, explained by architectural inductive biases, and explicitly not as evidence of recovering physical dynamics. Stitching compatibility is described as largely confined to families with similar latent geometry.
record.recipe_differences: Uses anchor-based relative embeddings and several similarity metrics to measure alignment across forecasters, plus a stitching evaluation; it does not reproduce a model-scale convergence sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment-estimate variability decreases as anchor count increases, with mean estimates approximately stable for K ≥ 16. Absolute similarity values vary by metric, although the paper reports stable qualitative family trends. Alignment also varies by architecture and dynamical system, including weaker RNN alignment on the Logistic Map.

fits_no_version.finding: Alignment of each forecaster's relative embedding with the relative geometry of observed trajectories varies by family and system (e.g., Lorenz: RNN 0.91, MLP 0.71, TF 0.73, ESN 0.34; Logistic map RNN 0.71). Accuracy can be high with low alignment (TF, ESN).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-to-data relative-geometry alignment depends on architecture and dynamics and dissociates from task accuracy.

record.problems: The main evidence concerns forecasting latent geometry on simulated systems; iEEG results are described as preliminary. Some family comparisons are qualitative or presented as figures, and the paper does not vary model scale, modality, training data, or objectives to identify their causal effects on alignment.
record.rows_left_out: Most per-model values from Tables 3 and 5–10 are omitted to stay focused on the claim and within the row limit; selected rows show representative alignment contrasts and the explicitly noted Logistic Map exception. The remaining table entries report additional model-by-system values. Figure-only visualizations of pairwise heatmaps and temporal profiles are not transcribed as separate rows.

untested.parts: No model size or capability sweep.
No vision or language models; no paired image–caption data.
No feature, unit or subspace comparison across seeds. Seed-to-seed relative-embedding similarity exists only in figures (see missing).
No linear maps, no unpaired-data mapping, no RNN/ESN stitching (excluded by design).
No interpretable features, neurons, SAE features or circuits.
No out-of-distribution inputs and no number-of-neighbours (mutual k-NN) setting.
No plateau with scale. Shared data or objective is not varied, so these are not isolated as causes; the authors attribute differences to architectural inductive bias.

missing.what: Cross-model similarity of absolute (non-relative) latents shows substantial misalignment, whereas relative embeddings show family structure. Apparent convergence depends on the representation used.

Input noise degrades alignment for all families (RNN alignment falls faster than performance). Input length L gives system-dependent alignment variability. Both show input dependence of measured alignment.
missing.locator: Section 5 'Noise and input length...'; Figure 2; Appendix Figure 6

missing.what: Within-architecture alignment across seeds: Figure 12 gives average cosine over 5 seeds, excluding the same seed. The text says RNNs show consistently high alignment across seeds and variants, while transformers are more variable.
missing.locator: Appendix Figure 12; Figure 1 heatmaps; Discussion paragraph on inductive biases

missing.what: Full Table 4 numeric stitching losses, including within-MLP-family variants (e.g., MLP enc→K-MLP dec relative 2.818 vs absolute 2.459, where relative is not better).
iEEG preliminary result showing qualitatively similar family-level cross-model alignment.

record.verdict_notes: Most rows (r1–r7, r9, r15) measure alignment to the true system's relative representation rather than between models, so they are delinked from V7. The reader's V6 'supports' label for the anchor sweep is reversed: the mean is stable for K≥16. The Table 4 text layout is flattened; only the cells that parse consistently with the authors' text are quoted. The models are small forecasters, not large foundation models, so the scale-based versions are out of reach.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size or capability scaling sweep, and no test of alignment rising with scale across independently trained models.
No vision-language models or paired image-caption inputs.
The study reports family-level alignment patterns, but does not test whether features or shared subspaces recur across seeds, or whether individual units/bases differ.
Tests stitching in this forecaster setup, not relative representations, layer stitching, or unpaired-data mapping in general.
No interpretable neurons, SAE features, or circuits are compared across models.
Tests anchor-count and similarity-metric choices; does not test out-of-distribution inputs or the number-of-neighbours setting.
Reports incomplete and family-dependent alignment, but does not isolate shared training data or objectives as causes, or test an alignment plateau across model scale.

rows.subject: Neural forecasters (MLP, RNN, Transformer, and ESN families; aggregate pattern)
rows.operation_detail: Compared cross-forecaster alignment patterns across systems using relative-embedding cosine similarity

conditions.value: Seven canonical synthetic systems; iEEG reported as preliminary external validation

rows.value: MLP variants form a cluster in all systems; RNN variants align in all systems except Logistic Map; Transformers tend to align less with other families; ESNs have lower alignment in several named systems.
rows.locator: Section 5, “Models form reproducible family-level alignment patterns”; Figure 1; Appendix Figures 4–5
rows.note: The text gives qualitative aggregate patterns rather than pairwise numeric values here. It also reports qualitatively similar family patterns in preliminary iEEG results.
rows.check: Correct link. Cross-forecaster heatmaps show within-family clusters (MLP; RNN except Logistic Map) and weaker transformer/ESN alignment with other families, despite shared data and objective. Values are figure-only.

rows.subject: Neural forecasters (aggregate across model families)
rows.operation_detail: Compared forecasting error with alignment to the true system
rows.measure: Relationship between forecasting MSE and representational similarity
rows.value: The relationship is generally positive but varies by model family and system; high predictive accuracy can coexist with low alignment, especially for Transformers and ESNs.
rows.locator: Section 5, “Forecast accuracy and representational alignment diverge across model families”; Figure 1
rows.note: The authors state that Transformers can have strong performance without strong alignment; no single aggregate correlation coefficient is given.
rows.check: Relates MSE to alignment with the true system; this is an accuracy–alignment link, not a cross-model convergence measure.

rows.subject: MLP and Transformer encoder–decoder pairs
rows.operation_detail: Swapped encoders and decoders using relative or absolute representations and measured H-step MSE
rows.value: Relative stitching outperforms absolute stitching within the MLP and Transformer families.
rows.locator: Section 5, “Latent stitching reveals family-specific representational compatibility”; Table 4
rows.note: The text states the comparison qualitatively. Table 4 reports pairwise values, but its flattened layout does not support assigning all values confidently.
rows.check: Value can be made numeric from Table 4 (relative vs absolute MSE): MLP enc→MLP dec 0.383 vs 1.655; TF enc→TF dec 0.043 vs 0.265. Note the Table 4 layout is flattened; these cells parse consistently.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5, latent stitching paragraph; Table 4: MLP→MLP absolute/relative MSE 1.655/0.383; TF→TF 0.265/0.043.

rows.subject: Transformer representations with MLP decoders
rows.operation_detail: Stitched Transformer representations to MLP decoders and compared relative with absolute stitching
rows.value: Relative stitching offers no benefit across families for Transformer representations mapped to MLP decoders.
rows.locator: Section 5, “Latent stitching reveals family-specific representational compatibility”; Table 4
rows.note: The text explicitly identifies this cross-family case as one where relative stitching does not help.
rows.check: Table 4 shows relative stitching is worse than absolute across families. TF enc→MLP dec is 2.019 vs 1.538; MLP enc→TF dec is 0.825 vs 0.293. Both are far above within-family relative losses (0.383, 0.043).

source_check.locator_found: Section 5, latent stitching paragraph; Table 4: TF→MLP absolute/relative MSE 1.538/2.019; MLP→TF 0.293/0.825.

rows.subject: MLP forecaster and true system
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of shared anchors and repeated alignment estimation with independently sampled anchors
rows.value: Mean approximately constant around r ≈ 0.74 once K ≥ 16; across-repeat variability decreases markedly as K increases.
rows.locator: Section 5, “Alignment estimates stabilize with increasing number of anchors”; Appendix Figure 9
rows.note: The paper fixes K = 80 for most experiments and K = 32 for stitching.
rows.check: The mean alignment is roughly constant (r≈0.74) for K≥16; only estimator variance shrinks with K. This shows little dependence on anchor count, contrary to V6. The reader's 'supports' label is wrong. The comparison is MLP vs true system, not model vs model.

source_check.correct: The experiment includes a random baseline using distinct anchor sets for the forecaster and true system; alignment is approximately zero across all K.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5, anchor-count ablation and following random-baseline paragraph; Appendix Figure 9.
source_check.problem: The baseline is recorded as not stated, although the paper explicitly reports a mismatched-anchor baseline.

rows.subject: Neural forecasters (aggregate across model families)
rows.operation_detail: Compared relative-space representations and forecast error over training

conditions.value: Multiple systems; Logistic Map is an exception for RNN alignment

rows.value: RNNs generally begin with comparatively high alignment and remain stable while test error decreases; MLP alignment is high from the beginning in several systems or rises with training in Lorenz-63 and double pendulum; Transformers have lower, more variable alignment while often achieving competitive or superior performance.
rows.locator: Section 5, “Forecast accuracy and representational alignment diverge across model families”; Figure 2
rows.note: This is a qualitative account of training trajectories; it does not test model-size scaling.
rows.check: Training-time trajectories of alignment to the true system, not cross-model alignment.

relationships.condition: Within-family relative stitching (MLP→MLP, TF→TF) on Lorenz-63
relationships.reason: Relative stitching cuts MSE versus absolute (0.383 vs 1.655; 0.043 vs 0.265), so encoders and decoders are interchangeable within a family (r10).
relationships.display_finding: Relative stitching reduced MSE from 1.655 to 0.383 for MLPs and from 0.265 to 0.043 for transformers.
